   falls back to the unmodified fit's - then the option buys fast sampling
   of a quantity that cannot be reported and slow effective sampling of the
   one that can. Computing the correction on the by-chain draws as well
   would settle it and costs one array reshape.
2. **The prior-weight diagnostic of Proposition 7.** $w$ is computable draw
   by draw from quantities already stored; reporting
   $\mathrm{ESS}(\{w\})$, or simply $\mathrm{sd}(\log w)$, converts
   Corollary 2's asymptotic argument into a per-fit check and would make
   the correction self-validating on designs and priors not covered here.
3. **The 100-replicate calibration run**, extended to the `mixing` design.
   The numbers in Section 9.1 come from 16 replicates; the larger run is
   confirmatory rather than decisive given the effect size, but `mixing`
   is genuinely new information: it is the design where the per-column
   search finds *nothing* for the slope column, so it exercises the full
   sequence - defect, repair, and correction - in one arm. Condition (S)
   has been verified to hold there ($3 \times 10^{-16}$), so the
   correction is applicable.
4. **Coverage of the other random-effects code paths**, per the second
   bullet of Section 9.2.

## 10. Related work summary

Section 2 covers this in full; in brief, this document sits at the
intersection of (a) general non-centered/centered reparameterization theory
for hierarchical models (Papaspiliopoulos & Roberts 2003; Papaspiliopoulos,
Roberts & Sköld 2007), (b) the specific geometric account of why this
matters for Hamiltonian/NUTS samplers (Betancourt & Girolami 2013;
Betancourt 2017; Hoffman & Gelman 2014; Neal 2003 for the related-but-
distinct funnel case), (c) the complementary account of why block/Gibbs
samplers are specifically vulnerable to the resulting growing correlation
(Roberts & Sahu 1997), and (d) applied precedent for this failure mode in
hierarchical Bayesian models generally (Ogle et al. 2020). Its contribution
is the specific diagnosis, source-verified mechanism, and replicated
empirical characterization of this problem for joint longitudinal-survival
models, and the finding that a substantial, previously unexplained part of
`jmjax`'s efficiency advantage over `JMbayes2` traces to this rather than to
covariate count as such.

## 11. Conclusion

`jmjax`'s regression-parameter efficiency advantage over `JMbayes2` is real,
large, statistically significant, replicated across simulated and (for the
`aids` dataset) genuinely independent real data, and mechanistically
understood down to the level of source code rather than only observed as an
aggregate benchmark number. It is best explained as the product of a
generic, well-documented sampler-class robustness (gradient-based HMC/NUTS
versus block-Gibbs/Metropolis) and a specific, targeted, verified
reparameterization of a real, diagnosed identifiability problem that recurs
- independently of covariate count - for any random slope on time. The
weaker, still-favorable nuisance-parameter comparison is better understood
as `JMbayes2`'s own degradation under growing inter-block correlation than
as an independent `jmjax` achievement.

The calibration question that the first draft named as the blocker has
been answered, and the answer is more interesting than a clean pass would
have been. The reparameterization miscalibrates the coordinates it
reports, exactly as its retracted predecessor did - but unlike that
predecessor it only *relocates* the uncertainty rather than destroying it,
and the relocation is invertible in closed form. A fit can therefore
sample in the well-conditioned geometry and report in the identified one,
which is what the option was always supposed to deliver and what it now
actually does. The remaining item before submission is narrow: the
effective sample size of the corrected estimand, which is the figure a
reader would quote and the last place the efficiency claim could still
come apart.

## 12. Note on publication venue

For the record, and as requested: this material is suited to a package
vignette regardless of any further venue (this document); beyond that, the
combination of a general, citable methodological contribution (Sections 2-
3, 8-9) with a software package it ships in and validates (Sections 5-7)
fits the scope of the *Journal of Statistical Software* or *The R Journal*
best (both have precedent for exactly this pairing - `JMbayes2` itself was
introduced this way). A parallel arXiv preprint (`stat.CO` or `stat.ME`) is
low-cost and would establish priority independently of review timelines.
`Bayesian Analysis`, `Statistics in Medicine`, and `Computational Statistics
& Data Analysis` are reasonable alternates if a narrower statistical-
methodology framing (rather than software-paper framing) is preferred.
Section 9's calibration gap, which an earlier draft flagged as the blocker
here, is now closed in both directions: the negative result is measured and
the correction is proved and validated (Sections 4.9 and 9.1). That
strengthens rather than weakens the submission - a reviewer in this area
would have asked for the coverage study, and the honest answer now comes
with a remedy attached rather than a caveat. The remaining item worth
having in hand first is the effective sample size of the corrected
estimand (Section 9.3, item 1), since the efficiency claim is the paper's
headline and `beta_corrected` is the quantity a reader would report.
